sections.html:
Carroll County is a small river county where the Kentucky River meets the Ohio. Carrollton, the county seat, sits right at that confluence, about 54 miles from Cincinnati and 55 from Louisville along U.S. 42, with Interstate 71 about four miles south of town. The 2020 count was 10,810 residents, and the 2025 estimate of 11,141 is 3.1 percent higher.

Median value for a house people live in is $140,900, and 65.7 percent of Carroll homes are owner-occupied. Monthly rent runs about $910. The county counted 4,736 homes in mid-2025 but issued only 1 building permit that year, so almost every buyer here is shopping resale. Many of them commute along the river or the I-71 corridor to jobs at employers such as North American Stainless, CertainTeed and Kentucky Utilities.

Low-lying lots near the rivers carry flood risk, and the worst flood on record hit in 1937. If your lot is close to the water, the city planning office can tell you where the floodplain line falls.

Who does what: the PVA values the parcel, the Sheriff's Office mails and collects, and the County Clerk gets the bill if it ends up delinquent. The clerk's counter also takes deeds, mortgages, wills and probate filings.

  • Sheriff: first floor of the courthouse at 440 Main Street, (502) 732-7010. Tax lookup and payment are online through the sheriff's page.
  • County Clerk: same building, (502) 732-7005, for delinquent taxes and deeds.
  • County administration: (502) 732-5448. This office edits or exonerates county tax amounts when a bill looks wrong.

Carroll's own FAQ puts the due date at December 31 and says to expect bills in October or November. No bill in hand? Search your parcel on the sheriff's page. The exact cutoff for the early-pay discount is printed on the bill itself, and the sheriff's office will confirm it by phone.

Timing is set by state law, KRS 134.015. Paying early earns a small discount. Paying late costs more at two separate points.

Carroll County payment timing
When you payWhat you owe
On or before the discount dateBill less 2%
Through December 31The printed amount
During JanuaryPrinted amount plus 5%
After January 31Printed amount plus 10%

Don't count on installments: the county takes the whole bill in one transaction. You can mix tender, though, such as a check plus cash or a card. A bill lost in the mail won't get your late fees waived under the state's administrative regulations, so chase it down yourself.

Unpaid tax turns into a lien, and a buyer's title search will find it. Ask the clerk for a payoff number as soon as you decide to list.

sections.h2: How a Carroll County tax sale works
sections.html:
Anything still unpaid on April 15 moves from the sheriff to the County Clerk. KRS 134.128 schedules the sale 90 to 135 days after that handoff, with owner notices at the 30 and 60 day marks.

Carroll's clerk holds the sale each summer in a second-floor courthouse room, starting in the morning. Outside bidders must sign up ahead of time. For this year's dates, phone (502) 732-7005.

Settle up before the sale. Even then the bill picks up interest, a clerk commission and a recording fee. Wait longer and the county attorney's commission, postage and advertising are added, and a certificate buyer can pile on more.

Step one is a conference with the PVA, step two is a filing with the clerk after the roll closes. The roll sits open for 13 days beginning the first Monday in May, and no appeal counts unless you've met with the PVA or a deputy.

Whenever the PVA assesses higher than the value you reported, you're owed a notice. A recent purchase helps: your deed price may become the value for the next January 1 if the house is unchanged, so hold on to the closing paperwork.

The county board must explain any change in writing, and you're allowed to record the hearing. Go. Skip the filing or the hearing and you lose any further review.

While the appeal is pending, keep paying on the value you reported. Ignoring the bill because a hearing is coming only adds penalties. If the board changes the number, you'll get a corrected bill.

Kentucky gives a break on the main residence of owners who are 65 or older or totally disabled. Form 62A350 handles either case, and the PVA has copies.

What comes off is a fixed dollar figure, not the whole assessment, and the state resets that figure every other year. It doesn't pass to a buyer. Owners with a total service-connected disability rating file once, as do owners found disabled by Social Security or the Kentucky Retirement System.

The PVA can give you the current dollar figure, because published numbers can trail a reassessment. If you're 65, make sure it was actually applied before you close.

Yes, you can sell with back taxes. The balance is subtracted from your sale price at the table, so no cash is needed up front. Typical steps:

  • Ask the sheriff for this year's balance.
  • Ask the County Clerk at (502) 732-7005 whether any earlier year went delinquent and for a payoff figure with fees.
  • Hand both numbers to whoever runs your closing.
  • Save your old purchase paperwork in case you appeal a value.
  • If a bill looks wrong, call county administration before paying, since that office can edit or exonerate county amounts.
  • Plan the closing date around the penalty dates, because the amount owed steps up on January 1 and again after January 31.

An as-is cash sale suits owners who can't wait on a lender, are settling an estate, or hold a rental with tenants inside. It skips repairs, showings and an appraisal, and can close before the next penalty date arrives.

In a standard sale the closing agent requests payoffs from the sheriff and clerk, pays them out of your price and records any release. Because values lock in on January 1, a bill can still show the prior owner's name after a mid-year sale. The year's tax should be split between you and the buyer as of the deed date.

For an office visit, carry your parcel number or street address, your deed if you have it, and the latest bill. If you're asking for a bill correction, the county administration office at (502) 732-5448 can tell you what proof it wants. For an exemption question, take photo ID and, for a disability claim, the letter from the agency that classified you.

Whichever way you sell, ask that the tax payoff and any lien release show up as separate lines on the final closing numbers.

faqs.q: What is the Carroll County tax deadline?
faqs.a: The annual due date is December 31. Bills paid by the early cutoff on your bill get 2 percent off, January adds 5 percent, and later payments add 10 percent.

faqs.q: Does Carroll County allow a payment plan?
faqs.a: No. The county requires the full amount in a single transaction, though check, cash and card can be combined.

faqs.q: Whom do I call about delinquent Carroll County taxes?
faqs.a: Phone the County Clerk at (502) 732-7005. That office collects delinquent real estate tax and runs the sale.

faqs.q: Is a late fee waived if my bill never came?
faqs.a: No, a bill that never arrived isn't grounds for a waiver. Each fall, look yours up on the sheriff's page.

faqs.q: Can a Carrollton house with back taxes be sold?
faqs.a: Yes. A buyer can purchase it as-is and the balance is paid from your proceeds. Get the number from the County Clerk before signing.
